summary_html: In Montana the **county attorney, attorney general, or an attorney hired by the county files the court petition** that opens an abuse and neglect case — CFSD does not file it, but the petition must be accompanied by a department affidavit (Mont. Code Ann. § 41-3-422(2)). Federal funding frameworks (IV-E/ASFA) link court oversight, reasonable-efforts findings, and permanency timelines to downstream actions.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E** — court findings; timelines; permanency planning  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal review of court/agency performance measures

primary_citations.citation_text: Montana - Title 41, Chapter 3 (Child Abuse and Neglect – mandatory reporting and protective services)

regulations_applicable.title: Department 37 - PUBLIC HEALTH AND HUMAN SERVICES

provisions_triggered.name: Due Process / Law of the Land

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: An interlocutory order granting temporary investigative authority and protective services is not appealable under Rule 1, M.R.App.P.; review must be sought by certiorari, habeas corpus or supervisory control, although the Court suspended the rules and reached the merits here because the parties had relied on a contrary prior statement.
key_cases.relevance: It is the leading Montana case on the form, content and reviewability of the initial child-protection petition.
key_cases.quote: We hold, therefore, that an interlocutory order granting temporary investigative authority and protective services is not appealable under Rule 1, M.R.App.P.

key_cases.holding: Termination was affirmed; the form of the petition did not preclude the district court from adjudicating the children youths in need of care when it did, and the findings established abuse or neglect by a preponderance of the evidence.
key_cases.relevance: It holds that the relief sought in the petition does not confine the court's power to adjudicate at the appropriate stage.
key_cases.quote: For a court to adjudicate a child a youth in need of care, the State must present evidence sufficient to establish that the child has been abused, neglected, or abandoned.

key_cases.holding: Termination was affirmed; a youth-in-need-of-care adjudication is not a prerequisite to temporary investigative authority under § 41-3-433 or to a court-ordered treatment plan under § 41-3-443(1) where the parents admit or stipulate to the allegations.
key_cases.relevance: It shows what relief a petition may seek and that the sequence of adjudication and treatment plan is not rigid.
key_cases.quote: a YINC adjudication is not always required for TIA and court-approved treatment plans

key_cases.holding: Termination of both parents' rights was affirmed; the district court retained jurisdiction even though it never entered a written order on the Department's timely petition to extend temporary legal custody, because § 41-3-442 contains no requirement that the court act within the six-month period and legislative filing or notice deadlines do not deprive courts of subject matter jurisdiction.
key_cases.relevance: It is the Montana holding that a district court's failure to observe the custody and extension deadlines in the dependency statutes does not divest it of subject matter jurisdiction over the petition, and it is the authority In re B.W.S. applies.
key_cases.quote: we hold that the District Court did have jurisdiction to terminate Father's parental rights

search_keywords: Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services

state_agency.name: Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services, Child and Family Services Division

statutory_basis.citation_text: Mont. Code Ann. § 41-3-422(2), (5)(a) — "The county attorney, attorney general, or an attorney hired by the county shall file all petitions under this chapter," accompanied by a department affidavit, and "the person filing the abuse and neglect petition has the burden": probable cause for emergency protective services, a preponderance for adjudication or temporary legal custody, a preponderance for long-term custody, clear and convincing evidence for termination

timeline_requirements.starts_from: Filing of the initial child abuse and neglect petition
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Statute states no penalty; an extension may be granted only on a showing of substantial injustice, and the court must then order an appropriate remedy that considers the best interests of the child (Mont. Code Ann. § 41-3-432(1)(c))
timeline_requirements.extension_grounds: Except as provided in the federal Indian Child Welfare Act or the Montana Indian Child Welfare Act (Title 41, ch. 3, pt. 13): stipulation of the parties under Mont. Code Ann. § 41-3-434, or a court-granted extension on a showing of substantial injustice under § 41-3-432(1)(a), (1)(c)
